extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and newspaper reporters/editors (readers of wartime news coverage)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and analyzing wartime events for a newspaper: factual dispatches (incidents, ship losses, rescues), tabulated 'box score' summaries, medical/disease reports, and signed editorial/analysis pieces. Emphasis on sourcing, specific details (ship names/tonnage/casualties), and interpretive context (weather, tides, invasion risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea warfare 'box score' reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish a tabulated 'box score' of sea warfare losses listing categories (subs, mines, other causes), numbers of vessels lost, dead, and reinforcements for a specified period (e.g., 'the 54th week of the war, from Sept. ... to Sept. 14, inclusive').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives a formatted example: 'THE FOLLOWING "BOX SCORE" LISTS SEA WARFARE LOSSES REPORTED DURING — THE’ 54TH WEEK OF THE WAR...' and includes totals by nation, grand totals and losses by nations (includes naval vessels). Use clear headings, breakouts by cause and by nation, and provide grand totals and context for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting war news — invasion-risk factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing invasion risk and operational timing, consider air war tactics, the calendar, moon phase, tides, weather and massing of forces as determinative factors ('Air war tactics, the calendar and new threats from Berlin combine to reinforce the warning in London that the next 48 hours is a "period of intense danger of invasion to England.'').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial recommends using meteorological and calendrical factors (full moon, highest tides) plus reports of ships, barges, airfields and troop concentrations to assess likelihood and timing of invasion. Analysts should weigh reported massing of men/ships/warplanes, airfield targets and supply concentrations when forecasting imminent threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing and explicit attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute facts and quotes to named sources (Associated Press, radio stations, naval authorities, purser, consul, medical officials), and indicate method of contact (e.g., 'The Associated Press spoke to him by radio telephone').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text include: 'The Associated Press spoke to him by radio telephone,' 'The announcement said,' and 'British consulate ... "We have absolutely no knowledge of those matters here; none whatsoever."' Always name the source, method (radio, statement, consulate), and note when officials or agencies issued apologies or denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed incident reporting (names, tonnage, casualties, locations, sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report incident specifics: vessel names and tonnage (e.g., '16,909-ton ship', '5,199-ton freighter S. S. Saint Agnes'), casualty counts, injuries, locations (off Oshima Island, off California coast), actions taken (rescues, surgeons sent aboard), and sequence/timing of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page illustrates including ship name, tonnage, number injured or rescued, how the incident occurred (e.g., 'dropped a test bomb ... injuring four Chinese in the crew'), whether there was structural damage, and subsequent movements (sailing for Vancouver, proceeding to Lisbon). Provide chronology and immediate official responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical and public-health wartime reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting diseases in war zones, include types of diseases reported (flu, cerebro-spinal meningitis, typhus, typhoid, smallpox, dysentery), treatment and preventive measures (e.g., sulfanilamide treatment), comparative statistics (deaths this year vs. previous year), expert commentary, and explanations of sanitation or public-health operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article supplies medical details and interpretation: cite physicians and health ministries, give numeric comparisons ('5,000 influenza deaths since January 41, 1940, against 3,500 in the same period of 1939'), describe preventive measures (evacuation, vaccination, delousing), and note factors limiting epidemics (better housing, food, medical units). Include sources and context for claims (which countries, occupied vs. unoccupied zones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of advance/special-service and dateline labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Label provisional or early copy with service and timing identifiers (e.g., 'SPECIAL NEWS SERVICE ADVANCE FOR AMS OF SUNDAY, SEPT. 15', 'By the Associated Press', 'Advance') to signal that the copy is an advance or special-service dispatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly uses 'SPECIAL NEWS SERVICE ADVANCE' and 'Advance' headings. Such labels inform editors and readers that material may be time-sensitive or preliminary; maintain those labels when reprinting and note any updates or corrections in later editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signed analysis/editorial separation and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly separate signed analysis or opinion pieces from straight news dispatches and frame them with author attribution and a distinctive headline (e.g., 'THE WAR TODAY by DEWITT MACKENZIE' or 'INTERPRETING THE WAR NEWS BY EDWARD E. POMAR').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page demonstrates authoritative analysis labeled by author; such pieces employ interpretation, historical analogy, and strategic judgment rather than only factual reporting. Maintain clear labeling so readers can distinguish facts from interpretation and opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note of censorship or publication control
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge when material has been censored, edited or passed by authorities for publication (e.g., 'the censor passed Dr. Bove's story for publication in Great Britain').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a dispatch mentions censorship, include that fact to inform readers of possible omissions or restrictions and to contextualize the report's completeness. Indicate which authority censored the material when known.
